structure.title: Persuading the conspirators
structure.text: Public celebration and private conversations establish the competing meanings of Caesar's growing power.

structure.title: Persuading the city
structure.text: The central political act shifts the problem from intention to public interpretation, alliance, and conflict.

people.name: Brutus
people.text: A noble Roman, admired for his honesty, who fears Caesar will make himself king and wonders whether he must act.

people.name: Cassius
people.text: A sharp, envious senator who works on Brutus's sense of honour to draw him into the plot.

people.name: Antony
people.text: Caesar's friend and loyal follower, a reveller whom the conspirators underestimate, and the best speaker in Rome.

context.title: Republican fear
context.text: The conspirators claim to defend shared government from one man's domination. That stated aim does not establish agreement about their methods.
context.takeaway: Separate political intention from public legitimacy.

context.title: Roman example
context.text: Shakespeare dramatises history rather than offering an unmediated record. The figures become competing examples of political conduct.
context.takeaway: Judge the play's presentation on its own terms.

notice.text: Compare private reasons with public speeches.
notice.why: An action needs a story that other people will accept.
A valued reputation can make someone easier to persuade.

opening: Brutus loves Caesar and fears what he might become. Persuaded that Rome’s freedom is at stake, he joins men planning to kill his friend before he can make himself a tyrant. Brutus believes his reasons will be enough to justify the deed to the people. But a city does not interpret a killing as neatly as a conspirator explains it, and Shakespeare gives the men fighting over Caesar’s legacy a weapon Brutus has dangerously underestimated: the power to tell the crowd what it has seen.
